strengths: Solid theoretical foundation: the paper generalizes projected DFM to probabilistic encoders/decoders (Propositions 3–5) with clear proofs, and derives data-conditional target rates for learnable insertion/unmasking schedules (Proposition 1) that provably generate the desired marginals via the KFE, including an ELBO-style guarantee (Proposition 5).

Practically attractive training procedure: the Kumaraswamy parameterization yields closed-form hazard rates and inverse-CDF sampling, and the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator allows joint training of generator and target-rate parameters with a single backward pass per sample (Algorithm 1), avoiding trajectory simulation.

The graph traversal experiments are informative and honest: the authors empirically expose a flexibility-vs-stability trade-off (trainable b_um destabilizes training, Figures 6/9), analyze the learned generation order quantitatively (correlation analysis, Figure 5), and clearly document that fixing b_um = 1 while retaining learnable insertion order gives the best results (87.9–88.1 exact match on hard vs 6.0–7.4 for FlexMDM).

De novo molecule generation shows consistent gains over FlexMDM in validity and quality across sampling budgets and nucleus settings (Table 2, Figure 7), with a fairly comprehensive hyperparameter sweep (auxiliary model size, confidence-based selection, p truncation) reported in full.

The paper maintains the same terminal time distribution as FlexMDM and reduces to it as a special case (Remark 1), making the contribution a clean, well-motivated extension rather than an ad hoc modification.
weaknesses: Limited empirical scope: experiments cover only one synthetic task (star graph traversal) and one domain (small molecules). No language/text experiments despite the insertion-based framing being motivated by sequence modeling, and no comparison against other order-learning or insertion baselines (ILM, EditFlows, Wang et al. 2025) empirically — only against FlexMDM, MDM, and ARM.

The headline claim of 'learnable order dynamics' is partially undercut by the method's own findings: the fully learnable target (both b_in and b_um trainable) is unstable and performs substantially worse (38.0 vs 87.9 hard exact match; 34.2 vs 87.9 shared), and even molecule experiments fix b_um = 1. In effect the deployed method learns only insertion timing, which narrows the contribution and suggests the joint learning objective needs further stabilization.

The practical gains on molecules are mixed: at default settings (p=1.0) validity is essentially unchanged (98.9 vs 99.0) and quality gains only materialize under aggressive nucleus truncation, at a cost to diversity (0.92 → 0.83–0.86) and uniqueness (96 → 79–87%). Baselines like SAFE-GPT and MDM remain competitive on the combined metric profile, and the FlexMDM+confidence configuration collapses (5.8 quality), which is reported but not explained.

The REINFORCE leave-one-out gradient estimator for φ is standard but its variance is not analyzed empirically, and the dependence of results on schedule regularization (Appendix D.5.2) and the regularization weight is not ablated.

Presentation issues: several typos ('have have', 'simultaneous simultaneous', 'exiting works', 'my replacing'), Table 5 is mislabeled as star-graph hyperparameters when it covers molecule generation, and the main text repeatedly references Figures 6/9 inconsistently. Some notation (sub/superscripts on λ, K, F) is dense and will slow readers.

No likelihood or calibration evaluation, and reproducibility rests on code links whose contents cannot be verified; run-to-run variance (±) is reported for molecules but not for the graph traversal results, where the gap between configurations (e.g., 38.0 vs 87.9) could partly reflect training instability.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and technically clean: injecting learnable, data-dependent hazard rates into the target rates of a variable-length masked DFM (FlexMDM) and showing that generator and target order dynamics can be trained jointly without simulating trajectories, using a single backward pass with a REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator (Eq. 12, Algorithm 1).

The theoretical development is careful: Propositions 1–6, the projected rate matching framework (Appendix C), and the Kumaraswamy parameterization that yields closed-form hazard rates (Eq. 10) and closed-form order probabilities (Prop. 6) are worked out in detail, and Remark 1 shows the method strictly generalizes FlexMDM.

The empirical ablations on graph traversal are informative and honest: the paper itself reports that a fully trainable unmasking rate destabilizes training (Fig. 6/9) and freezes b_um accordingly, and it dissects the learned order via correlation analysis (Fig. 5) rather than only reporting aggregate metrics.

The hard star-graph result is striking: exact match improves from 6.0/7.4 (FlexMDM) to ~88 (LFlexMDM), and the qualitative trajectory analysis (Figs. 4, 10, 11) supports that the model actually learns the locally optimal insertion order.
Additional nucleus-sampling sweeps, shared-backbone variants, and auxiliary-size ablations are provided (Tables 2, 7), improving transparency about design choices.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the motivating claims. Only two tasks are studied (star-graph traversal and de novo molecule generation with SAFE). No language modeling or text experiments are included, even though variable-length insertion modeling is primarily motivated by text-like sequence data (Section 1, Section 4). The generality of the contribution therefore remains untested on the domain that motivates it.

The headline molecule-generation comparison (Table 2) is confounded with sampling hyperparameters. FlexMDM is evaluated only at p=1.0, whereas LFlexMDM is swept over nucleus thresholds p ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0} and over auxiliary-network sizes, and the best tuned configuration is highlighted. The claimed 'significant improvements in validity and quality' therefore partly reflect sampling tuning rather than the learned order dynamics; Figure 7 (right) partially mitigates this but the main table's framing is asymmetric. The dramatic collapse of FlexMDM+confidence (validity 86.5, quality 5.8) is suspicious and not explained.

The order-learning story is less crisp than claimed: the strongest order correlation (-0.91, Fig. 5) is achieved in the configuration with trainable b_um that the authors themselves discard for instability; with the shipped configuration (frozen b_um) the correlation is only -0.60 and requires inference-time confidence-based position selection. The generator's performance gains in Table 1 come mostly from insertion-order learning, so the 'learnable order dynamics' narrative is weaker than the abstract implies.

The method adds a nontrivial auxiliary target-rate network (a separate transformer in the 'separate' setting) whose computational and parameter overhead is never quantified. The best configuration (frozen b_um, auxiliary-size small/xtiny) was selected using the graph-traversal task and then carried to molecule generation, risking hyperparameter transfer bias; the schedule regularization (D.5.2) adds further tuning surface without an ablation of its necessity.

No comparison against alternative gradient estimators or analysis of the variance of the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator (only n=2 samples, Eq. 12); given that φ is trained by a high-variance score-based estimator on top of an already-large action space, an ablation or variance study is needed to justify the design.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: repeated typos ('tokens is are', 'have have', 'exiting works', 'simultaneous simultaneous'), inconsistent naming (LFlexMDM vs LNFlexMDM), Tables 4 and 5 both captioned 'Hyperparameters for star graphs experiments' though Table 5 describes molecule generation, dangling/incomplete references (Huang et al., 2026; Schiff et al.), and a Figure 6/9 numbering mismatch. Number of random seeds and compute budget are not reported, which weakens confidence in small gaps (e.g., 93.0 vs 93.2 exact match).

Limitations discussion is minimal: the Future Work section is one sentence acknowledging efficiency, and the paper does not discuss the reduced diversity, the reliance on frozen b_um, or the applicability of the Kumaraswamy family (shared shape for insertion and unmasking, fixed a) as limitations of the learned order class.

strengths: Technically sound and well-grounded contribution: the paper derives tractable data-dependent target insertion/unmasking rates via projected discrete flow matching (Proposition 1 with full derivation in Appendix D.1), and shows the joint training of generator and target rates is feasible without trajectory simulation using a single backward pass (Proposition 5, REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator).

Meaningful empirical gains over the FlexMDM baseline: exact match on hard star graph traversal improves from 6.0% to 87.9% (Table 1), and molecule generation shows consistent quality improvements (~40% to ~60%+) and modest validity gains, with quality-vs-diversity and sampling-budget analyses (Figure 7).

Careful empirical study of design choices: the flexibility-vs-stability analysis (Figure 6/9, fixing b_um=1), shared vs. separate auxiliary backbones, and the generation-order correlation analysis (Figure 5) give insight into when and why learnable order helps.

The empirical finding that the model learns the locally optimal generation order on graph traversal (Figure 4, correlation approaching -1) provides direct evidence for the central claim rather than only downstream metrics.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly reports that fully trainable target rates destabilize training, motivates the schedule regularizer, and acknowledges the shared-backbone performance drop and the efficiency caveats in the Future Work section.
Comprehensive appendices (notation, proofs, gradient estimator derivation, Kumaraswamy closed forms, sampling algorithms, hyperparameters) plus project/code links support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core method is partially undermined by its own results: the unmasking rate b_um must be frozen (=1) for stable training and best performance, so the final model only learns insertion order; the title and abstract promise 'learnable order dynamics' more broadly, and a reviewer must take the reduced method on its own terms.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two tasks (synthetic star graphs and de novo small molecule generation) and one primary baseline (FlexMDM). No language/text experiments despite insertion-based generation being motivated largely by variable-length text; no comparison to EditFlows, ILM, or order-learning approaches like Wang et al. (2025).

Results depend on a fairly large hyperparameter search (auxiliary network size, confidence-based selection on/off, nucleus p, sampling steps), and the headline quality numbers come from the most favorable configurations (e.g., p=0.2), which reduces diversity; the baseline FlexMDM receives comparatively fewer tuning options.

REINFORCE-style gradient estimation for phi (Equation 12) likely has high variance, but no variance analysis, ablation on number of samples, or wall-clock/training-cost comparison against the FlexMDM baseline is provided; the auxiliary network adds nontrivial overhead.

Generality of the Kumaraswamy parameterization (fixed shared a constant, shape-constrained hazard) is not examined; sensitivity to a, the regularizer weights, and degenerate-schedule behavior are only addressed implicitly via D.5.2.

Presentation issues: several typos ('the dependencies in the tokens is are', 'have have', 'exiting works', 'simultaneous simultaneous'), inconsistent model naming (LFlexMDM vs. LNFlexMDM in Appendix Tables 4-5), a duplicated reference (Lipman et al. 2024a/b), and repeated table captions slightly weaken polish.

Claims like 'significant improvements in validity' should be tempered: validity gains over FlexMDM are small (98.9% to ~99.5-99.9%), with the more convincing improvement being quality; uniqueness drops notably with confidence-based decoding.
